newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan urges China to resume talks on hijackers.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan urges China to resume talks on hijackers.

text.p: Taiwan on Tuesday urged rival China to resume long-stalled talks on repatriating mainland hijackers a day after Chinese security personnel foiled a hijacking of a domestic airliner carrying Taiwan tourists.

On-board security officials halted a bid to commandeer a mainland jet on Monday on a flight between Wuhan in central Hubei province and the southern city of Zhuhai bordering Portuguese-run Macau, Taiwan passengers said.
Hong Kong's China-controlled Wen Wei Po confirmed witnesses' reports that the plane landed in Guangzhou, capital of southern Guangdong province, and the aircraft and passengers were safe.
Mainland officials had yet to comment on the incident.
Some 38 Taiwan passengers who witnessed the incident on board a China Northwestern Airlines plane described the scene after returning on Tuesday to Taipei's international airport.
"The plane was very unstable (in the air). Several people were fighting in the front row of the aircraft and then the hijacker was subdued," one eyewitness told state radio.
Another eyewitness said the hijacker claimed to be carrying a suitcase with explosives.
Taiwan's top China policymaker, Chang King-yuh, expressed his concern over the incident and urged Beijing as soon as possible to resume long-stalled talks on repatriation of mainland hijackers.
"We hope to hold talks with the mainland side on the repatriation of hijackers, but so far communist China is still unwilling to resume talks to discuss such issues," Chang said.
"We hope the mainland side can practically face this sort of problem," he added.
China has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war separated them in 1949.
Taiwan and China reached a semi-official accord in January 1995 on repatriating hijackers and illegal immigrants fleeing to Taiwan, but the agreements have not been signed.

China indefinitely suspended semi-official talks with Taiwan in mid-1995 after President Lee Teng-hui made a private but high-profile visit to the United States. Beijing interpreted the trip as an attempt to promote Taiwan's independence.
Chinese airlines suffered a spate of hijackings two years ago, mainly by people trying to flee to Taiwan, prompting a strengthening of what had been lax security at domestic airports.
